title: Parting with kindness
hookLine: even divorce comes with limits, a waiting period and kindness (65:1–2)

cards: Most endings are messy. A friendship goes quiet. A job ends with a badge handed back at a desk.
A marriage ends with lawyers, or silence, or a slammed door. When things fall apart, manners tend to go first. Now open the sixty-fifth surah of the Qur'an.
Its name is at-Talaq, divorce. A whole chapter named for an ending, and the first thing it does is slow everything down. Count the days.
Don't push anyone out of the house. Bring witnesses. Be kind on the way out the door.

teach.b: The surah opens by speaking to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and through him to everyone. When you divorce, it says, do it with regard to the waiting period, the 'iddah, and count it carefully.
During that time, don't turn the women out of their houses, and they shouldn't leave, except in a case of open indecency.

teach.h: THESE ARE THE LIMITS OF ALLAH.
teach.b: Then a phrase the Qur'an uses elsewhere too: these are the limits of Allah, the hudud, and whoever oversteps them has wronged his own soul.
Verse one ends with a quieter line: you don't know, perhaps Allah will bring about something new after this. The waiting period isn't only paperwork. It's a pause.
Two people under one roof, still, with time to cool down, and maybe to change their minds. Verse two says what happens when the waiting is over.

teach.h: KEEP OR PART: BOTH IN KINDNESS.
teach.b: Either keep them in kindness, or part from them in kindness. The Arabic is bi-ma'ruf: in the way that's recognized as right, decent, fair. Both doors, staying and leaving, carry the same word.
And bring two just witnesses, so nobody can later rewrite what happened. The schools of Islamic law work out the details differently: how the waiting is counted, whether the witnesses are required.
But the shape is shared. Even the end of a marriage has limits. Even a parting has manners.
The Qur'an doesn't pretend divorce never happens. When it does, the one walking away still owes the other decency.

how: In Islamic law divorce is permitted but hedged with rules: a waiting period ('iddah) during which, in a revocable divorce, the wife normally stays in the home, the option of reconciliation, witnesses, and the instruction that a couple either stay together or part bi-ma'ruf, in kindness. The schools of law differ on details.

o: what's recognized as right and decent
the limits God sets on a marriage
the waiting period after a divorce

games.q: parting with kindness — tap the pairs.
p: in kindness, the way known to be right

s: the Qur'an has a whole surah named for divorce
surah 65, at-Talaq, opens with the rules for it.
in 65:1 the wife must leave the house at once
the verse says not to turn her out during the waiting period.
the verse says perhaps something new will come after
the waiting period leaves room for a change of heart.

games.q: a marriage is ending. the waiting period has begun. by 65:1, where does the wife live while it runs?
o: she goes to her family by law.
games.why: she stays. the verse forbids turning her out, and adds: perhaps Allah will bring about something new after this.

practice: Pick one thing that's ending, big or small: a conversation you keep cutting off, a group chat you've been ghosting, a project that's done.

Picture the ending you'd be glad to have given: a clear word, no slammed door, nothing taken that isn't yours. If an ending in your life was hard, let it be hard, and just notice what kindness would have looked like.

wordCard.voice: Ma'ruf: what's recognized as right and decent, the word Surah At-Talaq uses for how a marriage should both continue and end. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: in kindness, in the way recognized as right. 65:2 uses it for staying and for parting alike.

carryVoice: Your line: part with kindness. Even an ending can be decent, and kind. Until next time.
